title: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) Service Extension for Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs)
summary: Defines an extension to SMTP that lets a client request Delivery Status Notifications. The client can say when notifications should be generated, whether the original content should be returned, and attach extra information so the sender can identify which recipient and transaction a notice refers to.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3461 extends SMTP so a sender can request delivery status notifications for individual recipients. It also carries identifiers that help match a report to the original recipient and mail transaction.

questions: how to request a dsn in smtp
what does notify=never mean in smtp
subtitle: How SMTP senders request delivery reports and control the information those reports contain.

tldr.problem: Traditional SMTP failure notices could omit which recipient or mail transaction had a problem, and systems lacked a common way to exchange delivery reports.
tldr.mechanism: The DSN extension adds NOTIFY and ORCPT parameters to RCPT and RET and ENVID parameters to MAIL. These specify when notices are requested, what recipient and transaction identifiers they carry, and how much message content to return.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3461 obsoletes RFC 1891. It is a Draft Standard updated by RFC 3798, RFC 3885, RFC 5337, RFC 6533, and RFC 8098.

today: RFC 3461 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1891. It has been updated by RFC 3798, RFC 3885, RFC 5337, RFC 6533, and RFC 8098.

sections.title: Why Delivery Reports Needed More Detail
sections.content:
SMTP servers report when they cannot deliver a message to one or more recipients. Traditional notices were ordinary email messages, and experience with large mailing lists showed that they could be too vague to identify the host or recipient involved.

RFC 3461 defines an SMTP extension for Delivery Status Notifications (DSNs). It aims to give senders a clear result, preserve enough information to identify the transaction and recipient through forwarding, and avoid generating further DSNs when a DSN itself fails.

The DSN message format is defined by a separate specification. This RFC defines how an SMTP sender requests notifications and how mail transfer agents handle those requests.
sections.plainLanguage: A failure notice needs to identify which recipient and message it concerns. This extension lets SMTP carry the details needed to create a useful delivery report.

sections.title: Checking for DSN Support
sections.content:
An SMTP client checks support by sending EHLO. If the server responds with code 250 and includes the DSN keyword, it supports this extension. The keyword has no parameters.

The extension adds no SMTP commands. It adds NOTIFY and ORCPT to RCPT, and RET and ENVID to MAIL. A supporting server must not reject a command just because a valid DSN parameter is present or absent.

When relaying to another supporting server, a mail transfer agent generally passes the sender's requests onward. If it hands mail to a different kind of system, it makes a best effort to honor them.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first checks whether the server advertises DSN support. If it does, the client can add notification options to the existing mail commands.

sections.title: The Four DSN Parameters
sections.content:
NOTIFY is attached to a recipient and controls when a report may be sent: SUCCESS, FAILURE, or DELAY. NEVER requests no report and must appear alone. If NOTIFY is absent, the server may use failure-only notifications or failure and delay notifications.

ORCPT carries the original recipient address, which may differ from the current address after forwarding. RET asks for the full message or only its headers in a failure report. ENVID carries a sender-chosen identifier that is returned with reports so the sender can match a report to a mail transaction.

ORCPT and ENVID values use xtext encoding to represent characters that SMTP parameters cannot carry directly. Their decoded values must consist of printable US-ASCII characters. A command must not repeat its DSN parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipient options select when to report and preserve the original address. The message options identify the transaction and say whether a failure report should include the whole message or only its headers.

sections.title: Relaying and Delivery Rules
sections.content:
When relaying to a server that supports DSN, the mail transfer agent carries forward any supplied ENVID, RET, NOTIFY, and ORCPT values according to the RFC's rules. If the next server does not support DSN, it must not send those parameters; the relaying agent handles the requested notices itself.

For local delivery, success means that the message is placed in the mailbox or made available through a mail-access service, not that the recipient has read it. The agent sends success or failure reports according to NOTIFY. Delay reports are optional, but must not be sent if the sender explicitly excluded delays.

A DSN must not be sent for a message with a null SMTP return address. The MTA should instead notify the local postmaster through a method that does not create another DSN.
sections.plainLanguage: If the next mail server cannot handle DSN requests, the current server takes responsibility for the requested reports. A successful delivery means the message reached the mailbox or mail-access service.

sections.title: Forwarding, Aliases, and Mailing Lists
sections.content:
An alias keeps the original envelope return address when it forwards mail. A mailing list changes that address to the list administrator, so reports about delivery to list members go to the administrator rather than the original sender.

Delivery to a list's submission address counts as final delivery for the original message. When the list redistributes the message, its DSN parameters must not be copied from the original message. For a single-recipient alias, DSN parameters should usually be passed on without issuing a separate report.

For an alias with multiple recipients, the RFC permits different handling choices, including issuing a relayed or expanded report. Treating a forwarding address like a mailing list can keep the forwarding address confidential.
sections.plainLanguage: A mailing list becomes responsible for reports about copies it sends to its members. This can also keep a recipient's private forwarding address from being exposed to the original sender.

sections.title: The Contents of a DSN
sections.content:
A DSN is a MIME report with content type multipart/report and report type delivery-status. It contains a human-readable explanation, a structured message/delivery-status part, and the original message or a portion of it.

When the sender requests RET=FULL, the full message should be returned with failure reports, though the MTA may return only headers if the message exceeds an implementation-specific length. A report with no delivery failures should return only headers.

The structured part includes reporting and final recipient details, an action, and a status. It also carries the original envelope identifier and original recipient when those were supplied. SMTP-generated DSNs use a null reverse path and cannot request further reports.
sections.plainLanguage: A DSN combines a readable explanation, structured delivery details, and some or all of the original message. The format also prevents a report from triggering another report.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says this extension does not by itself change SMTP's basic security properties. It adds implementation complexity, which increases the risk of mistakes.

Earlier notification schemes could create storms of reports when they interacted unexpectedly with mailing-list software. The rules for success notifications are designed so that a correct implementation avoids that interaction. The RFC also points to separate security guidance for report messages and DSNs.
sections.plainLanguage: The extension adds rules that software must implement correctly. Its mailing-list rules are designed to prevent one delivery report from triggering a flood of more reports.

items.label: No report
items.desc: Do not return a DSN under any condition; this value appears alone.

items.label: Successful delivery
items.desc: Request a DSN when delivery succeeds.

items.label: Failed delivery
items.desc: Request a DSN when delivery fails.

items.label: Delayed delivery
items.desc: Allow a DSN when delivery is unusually delayed.
